newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian central bank sees room for growth.
newsitem.headline: Australian central bank sees room for growth.

text.p: Australia's central bank, the Reserve Bank of Australia, is confident it has inflation under control and now sees room for faster economic growth.
"Can we grow faster? We probably can, given the spare capacity in plants and in the labour market," Reserve Bank Governor Bernie Fraser told a parliamentary economic committee on Thursday.
As new data showed a sharp rise in joblessness, Fraser said the bank was more confident about the inflation outlook than it was about economic growth and unemployment.
Inflation and the current account deficit on the balance of payments were Australia's traditional constraints on growth.
"They're not constraints at the moment," said Fraser, who retires next week.
His replacement, Deputy Governor Ian Macfarlane, was also confident on inflation.
Fraser said government inflation forecasts -- for 2.75 percent core inflation by mid-1997 -- were a little pessimistic.

"The growth forecasts are underpinned by a reasonably encouraging outlook for our major trading partners, good levels of business and consumer confidence and the absence of any major imbalances in the domestic economy," he said.
But he was still concerned about unemployment, which appears to have stalled near 8.5 percent lately.
"On inflation, we're a bit more confident about what might happen over the next six or 12 months than we are about what might happen to growth and employment."
Fraser has always cited unemployment as one of his greatest concerns as central bank governor.

He said on Thursday that unemployment had been one of main reasons why the bank had carried out its surprise monetary easing on July 31, when it dropped overnight cash rates to 7.0 percent from 7.5 percent.
Macfarlane, who takes up duties as governor next week, said that it would be extremely unfortunate if trade union wage claims were inconsistent with the RBA's inflation target.
But he added: "I don't think that they will."
However, growth alone would not be enough to reduce unemployment to more acceptable levels, although Fraser did not specifically nominate a Reserve Bank target employment level.

"Even when you've got a good sustained rate of growth going, I suspect that that's not going to be enough to reduce unemployment to the level that we'd like to see it reduced to, whatever that might be, whether it's six (percent) or five or four or whatever," Fraser told the parliamentary committee.
"And that's because the jobs might be there, but the people who are unemployed mightn't have the skills or the experience of whatever to make a contribution," he said.
Figures released while Fraser was before the committee showed Australia's unemployment rate rose to 8.8 percent in August, the highest rate since April, from 8.5 percent in July.

The favourable moderation in inflation and wages growth, and the stalling in the unemployment rate at around 8.5 percent were mentioned by the bank as factors in its decision to cut interest rates on July 31 by 0.5 percentage points to 7.0 percent.
